title: Whittled walnut pendant
subtitle: A small carved pendant blank for a cord or chain
excerpt: A small teardrop pendant in seasoned walnut: 4 cm at its longest, 2.5 cm wide, 8 mm thick, drilled for a cord. Detail-knife work for the shaping, danish-oil finish. An intermediate project because the small scale requires controlled short strokes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
A section of wood where the grain direction runs across the narrow dimension of the piece, leaving only a short fibre length supporting the section. Short grain is fragile.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and spoon-carving.

content.text: A pendant blank is a small shaped piece drilled through the top for a cord or chain. At 4 cm long and 2.5 cm wide, it is the smallest project in this whittling series. The small scale makes it intermediate: every cut must be short and controlled, there is no room to correct an over-cut, and the narrow drilling point at the top is
short-grain
and fragile. The project uses
seasoned wood
walnut for its colour: dark brown with a tight grain that takes a very fine knife finish and looks distinguished even without a thick coating.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
Wood
Walnut in the
seasoned

state. A 6 cm length from a 10 mm-thick walnut board, or a 10 mm-thick walnut turning blank, provides the starting piece. Walnut is dense, fine-grained, and cuts cleanly under a sharp detail knife. Its dark colour hides small tool marks that would show clearly on a pale wood. Ebony or rosewood would be alternatives but are harder to source sustainably; padauk cuts similarly to walnut and turns orange-red when oiled.
Tools
Sloyd knife
: bulk shaping.
Detail knife: all finish cuts on this scale.
Leather strop: strop before every series of cuts on walnut.
Danish oil: brings out walnut's deep colour without adding a thick plastic layer.
Method
Step 1: Mark and cut the teardrop outline

Draw the teardrop on the blank: wide curve at the bottom, narrowing to a flat 5 mm section at the top where the cord hole will be drilled. Use the sloyd knife on the straight cuts, the detail knife on the curves. At this scale, all cuts should be 10 to 15 mm long at most.
Step 2: Thin the edges

Reduce the edge of the pendant to 3 mm all around, with the face slightly domed and the back flat. This gives the pendant a lens-profile in cross-section: thin and light, but not fragile. The detail knife handles the edge thinning at this scale. Short strokes only, working from the widest point of the pendant outward to the edge.
Step 3: The cord hole
Drill a 2 mm hole through the flat top section of the pendant, 3 mm from the top edge, centred. The flat top section is the most
short-grain
part of the piece. Drill slowly and with the blank supported firmly to prevent the bit breaking out on exit. A 2 mm hole accepts a 1 mm cord or a fine chain.
Step 4: Final knife-finish pass

With the cord hole drilled, use the detail knife to remove any drill-exit tearout and to refine the surface. This final pass should remove only the thinnest shaving, less than 0.3 mm. The knife finish on walnut is very clean when the edge is properly stropped and the stroke is controlled.
Finishing

Apply danish oil with a fingertip or a small cloth patch. The small size means the oil soaks in within ten minutes. Two coats are enough. Cure for five days. Walnut with danish oil produces a deep, warm brown that resembles the look of a much thicker finish without any coating.
Variations
Burn a simple design into one face before oiling using a pyrography pen.
A different silhouette: an oak leaf in maple, a crescent moon in walnut, a simple disc.
Make a batch of twelve from offcuts: they cost almost nothing in material and make excellent gifts.

attrs.symptom: The top section snapped at the cord hole
attrs.cause: Too little material above and below the hole, or the bit was pushed too fast on exit.
attrs.fix: Make sure there is at least 3 mm of wood above the hole and 3 mm to each side. Drill at low speed and support the blank from underneath on the exit side.

attrs.symptom: The detail knife is tearing the walnut surface
attrs.cause: The edge is not sharp enough or the cut is against the grain.
attrs.fix: Strop before the final pass. If tearing persists, reverse the cut direction.
